newsitem.title: JAPAN: North Korean ruling elite tells of rift.
newsitem.headline: North Korean ruling elite tells of rift.

text.p: A rift between North Korea's civilian and military leadership threatens the future of peace talks, a group of U.S. senators said on Saturday.

Senator Ted Stevens (R-Alaska), leader of a group of five senators just returned from a 24-hour visit to the North Korean capital Pyongyang, told a news conference in Tokyo that civilian authorities had spoken openly of a split with the military over the issue of international aid and peace talks.

Stalinist North Korea has been devastated by two years of floods, creating serious food shortages. The military is demanding food and other aid before full talks take place to formally end the Korean War.

"I think that we were led to believe that there is a rift. The military is disturbed that the civilian authorities have not been able to obtain the food and fuel they'd been told they'd get," Stevens said.
Senator Pete Domenici (R-New Mexico) said civilian authorities warned of a possible reaction from the military if their demands for aid were not met.

"They were open in saying that if they were unable to get food supplies they were not sure how the military would respond to participation in the four-party peace talks ... It wasn't anything said secretly. It was both said very openly and forthrightly," Domenici said.
The talks would involve the two Koreas plus China and the United States.

The senatorial delegation met with Korean First Vice Foreign Minister and Vice-chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee Kang Sok-ju during their visit but was not able to meet any military officials despite requests by U.S. officials.

U.S. Vice-President Al Gore discussed ways to convince North Korea to join the talks with South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Saturday, after a five-day visit to China during which he discussed the talks with Chinese President Jiang Zemin, U.S. officials said.
Pyongyang has made its first formal response to the call for talks by insisting the United States and South Korea promise first to supply it with substantial food aid.
U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Bill Richardson on Friday rejected a North Korean demand for more food aid as a condition for taking part in the talks.
However, Richardson predicted the international community might respond more positively to North Korea's needs if it joined the talks.
International aid agencies say North Korea is facing a serious food shortage.
